author: Claude (English teacher role), v2 after expert audit
basis: Rewritten against the v2 quality gate after two independent expert audits (CEFR assessor; speech coach + fact checker) found the v1 text passed on averages while individual slides missed their band, A2 and B1 were the same sentences with synonyms swapped, and several facts had drifted. Facts corrected to source: +1.6 degrees over a century (NSTC 2024) against a global 1.3; Climate Change Response Act 2023; carbon fee live 2025; Taichung capture demonstration about 2,000 t/yr, not a deployed solution; public transport share is about 14%, so 'we rely on public transport' was removed; 'Silicon Shield' dropped as a cross-strait deterrence term unsuited to a climate talk. Level is carried by syntax and lexical load, not by word count.

slides.1: Something has shifted in the way our seasons behave, and the record heat, sudden flooding and vanishing winters are no longer unusual events. They are the local signature of a global emergency.
slides.2: The thirteenth global goal asks every government to reduce emissions and to build genuine defences against disaster. Taiwan, although excluded from the United Nations, has chosen to meet the identical standard.
slides.3: Geography leaves us very little margin. We are a crowded island on the typhoon track, with a low western coastline and an export-driven economy built around power-hungry manufacturing that never stops.
slides.4: Consider the measurements rather than the impressions. A century of observations shows Taiwan warming by 1.6 degrees against a global 1.3, positioning our island among the faster-warming regions of the planet.
slides.5: Our difficulty is structural rather than moral. Coal and imported gas still dominate electricity generation, and the chip industry that underwrites our prosperity cannot lose even a single hour of supply.
slides.6: Two uncomfortable questions follow from that. If industrial demand keeps climbing, can clean power ever really overtake it, and if it cannot, which generation absorbs the debt we are quietly building?
slides.7: Progress has nonetheless been substantial. The 2023 Act wrote net zero by 2050 into statute, and a carbon fee introduced in 2025 now bills the largest emitters for what they release.
slides.8: Two industries now mark our shoreline. Offshore turbines face the Strait in their hundreds, while solar panels have occupied campus roofs, aquaculture ponds and industrial parks the length of the island.
slides.9: Public effort here is genuine but not enough. Recycling rates beat those of most economies, yet private scooters still rule everyday travel, so personal habit cannot substitute for structural reform.
slides.10: Engineers are rebuilding the grid around software rather than switchgear. The intention is that a program allocates power minute by minute, and Taipower has moved from modelling into limited trials.
slides.11: Carbon capture illustrates both the promise and the proportion of this work. A demonstration unit at Taichung removes roughly 2,000 tonnes a year, which validates the chemistry while remaining tiny beside the output of the plant.
slides.12: Urban travel offers a more convincing example. Electric scooters manufactured here operate on a battery exchanged in seconds, and thousands of swap points now form a refuelling network of national scale.
slides.13: Cutting carbon nevertheless imposes real costs on the smallest firms. Cleaner gear needs money that small factories seldom hold, so a transition designed without support will simply move the hardship elsewhere.
slides.14: Energy security remains politically unresolved. Precision factories demand power every hour, whereas wind and solar output rises and falls, forcing a hard choice between more gas and a nuclear restart.
slides.15: The atmosphere ignores sovereignty entirely. Taiwan holds technology worth sharing, yet exclusion from the main climate talks limits how far that knowledge can in practice travel beyond our own shores.
slides.16: Scepticism is a civic skill worth practising. Companies now market their green virtue while altering very little, so insist on audited figures and dated promises rather than photographs of turbines.
slides.17: The direction is encouraging without yet being sufficient. The law exists, offshore capacity is expanding and the first capture trials have begun, yet renewable generation still sits below our own target.
slides.18: This concerns you considerably more than it concerns me. Your cohort will supply the engineers, voters and consumers of the coming decades, and those choices will outlive every administration now in office.
slides.19: Despair is analytically useless here, whereas curiosity is genuinely productive. So interrogate the science, verify the figures you are given, and communicate whatever you establish as clearly as you can.
slides.20: Which returns the question to this room: will your generation merely inherit this transition, or will you actually engineer it? Taiwan is ready to deliver on SDG 13, and I have personally decided that I am.
